## Zone-2 verdicts

**A2.1 - the proposed direction works.** Resolving to indices first and building the touched set from `table[index].id` closes it, and disturbs nothing: the full 1018-test suite passes, including every pre-existing `#13435` atomicity test.

**A2.2 - `bulkDelete` genuinely CANNOT misbehave this way.** Not symmetry-by-assertion; the reason is structural. `bulkDelete` performs exactly **one** id comparison (the resolving `findIndex`), and everything downstream is keyed on that comparison's **result** - a table index - never on caller input. There is no second lookup to disagree with the first. That also makes its de-dup type-proof: `['1', 1]` against a stored `1` collapses to one index. Had the set been keyed on caller ids, those would be two entries and the two splices would remove index 0 twice, taking a neighbouring row with it. Both properties are now pinned by test rather than left to inspection. No change made to `bulkDelete`.

**A2.3 - `exceptId` filtering is STRICT** (`row.id === exceptId` in `assertNoUniqueViolation`). It is unaffected here because `bulkUpdate` already passed the **stored** `table[index].id` rather than the caller's id, so self-exclusion was type-consistent. Worth recording: passing caller input there would have been a second instance of this same class. `exceptId` also cannot mask the defect, since it excludes only the row being checked, never a sibling row of the same batch.
